lessons.title: Determining When Seedlings Are Ready
lessons.body:
Seedlings are ready to transplant when they have 4 to 6 true leaves, not just the first two seed leaves. For most vegetables like tomatoes, peppers, and cabbage, this happens 3 to 5 weeks after sowing, depending on weather. In hot areas, it may be faster; in cool highlands, slower. The stem should be as thick as a pencil lead, and the roots should hold the soil together when you gently lift the seedling. If roots are circling the bottom of the tray, it's time to move them.

Check the roots by sliding a seedling out of its cell. Healthy roots are white and firm. If they are brown or mushy, you have root rotâdiscard those seedlings. For trees like mango or avocado, wait until the seedling is 30 to 45 cm tall and has a woody stem before transplanting to the field. For onions, transplant when they are 15 cm tall and as thick as a pencil.

Do not wait too long. Overgrown seedlings become leggy, and their stems may bend or break during transplanting. They also compete for light and nutrients, leading to weak plants. A simple test: hold the seedling by its true leaf and liftâif the root ball stays intact, it's ready. If it crumbles, wait a few more days and water less to encourage root binding.

Weather matters. Transplant on a cloudy day or in the late afternoon to reduce stress. Avoid transplanting during heavy rain or hot midday sun. In dry areas, transplant after a good rain when soil is moist. If you must transplant in hot weather, shade the seedlings for the first few days.

Finally, harden off seedlings before transplanting (see next lesson). A seedling that has been hardened can be transplanted a bit earlier. Always transplant at the same depth as in the nurseryâexcept tomatoes, which can be buried up to the first true leaves to grow more roots.

lessons.title: Hardening Off Techniques
lessons.body:
Hardening off is the process of gradually exposing seedlings to outdoor conditions so they can survive the shock of transplanting. Start hardening off 7 to 10 days before you plan to transplant. If you skip this step, your seedlings may wilt, scorch, or die within hours of transplanting.

Begin by reducing water. Water half as much as usual, but do not let plants wilt completely. This encourages roots to grow deeper. On day 1, place seedlings outdoors in a shaded, protected spot for 2 hours. Bring them back indoors or under cover. On day 2, leave them out for 3 hours. Increase by 1 hour each day until they stay out all day. By day 5, expose them to morning sun for 2 hours, then shade. By day 7, they can take full sun for 4 to 6 hours if temperatures are mild.

If you don't have a greenhouse, use a simple shade net (50% shade) or a tree. In very hot areas, harden off in the evening or early morning to avoid scorching. For cool highlands, gradually expose to cooler nights. If frost is forecast, bring seedlings in or cover with a blanket.

Reduce watering during hardening, but never let the soil dry completely. On the last day, water thoroughly before transplanting to help the root ball hold together. Do not fertilize during hardeningâit can burn stressed roots.

For seedlings grown in trays, you can also harden by moving them to a raised bench or closer to the edge of the shade. For bare-root seedlings (like some trees), hardening is done by root pruning: cut the taproot with a sharp spade 10 cm below the soil surface, 2 weeks before lifting. This forces fibrous roots. Always water after root pruning.

A well-hardened seedling has a thicker stem, darker leaves, and roots that hold soil. It may be slightly shorter than unhardened ones, but it will establish faster and yield more.

lessons.title: Transplanting to Field or Larger Containers
lessons.body:
Transplanting is best done in the late afternoon or on a cloudy day. Water the seedlings thoroughly 2 hours before lifting. Prepare the planting hole the same depth as the root ball and twice as wide. For field planting, space according to crop: tomatoes 60 cm between plants and 90 cm between rows; cabbage 45 cm by 60 cm; peppers 45 cm by 60 cm; onions 10 cm by 20 cm. For trees, dig a hole 30 cm deep and 30 cm wide.

If transplanting to larger containers, choose a pot at least 5 cm wider than the current one. Use a potting mix of 3 parts soil, 1 part compost, and 1 part sand or rice husk. Fill the pot one-third, place the seedling, then fill around the roots, firming gently. Leave a 2 cm gap at the top for watering.

Handle seedlings by the leaves, not the stem. A crushed stem kills the plant. For tray seedlings, push from the bottom and lift the root ball. For bare-root seedlings, keep roots moist and spread them in the hole. For tomatoes, bury the stem up to the first true leaves to grow more roots. For other crops, plant at the same depth as before.

After placing, fill the hole with soil and press firmly to remove air pockets. Water immediately with 1 to 2 litres per plant. If the soil sinks, add more soil. For containers, water until it drains from the bottom. Mulch around the plant with dry grass or leaves, keeping mulch 5 cm away from the stem to prevent rot.

In dry areas, dig a small basin around each plant to hold water. In windy areas, stake tall seedlings like tomatoes. If transplanting into black plastic mulch, cut a hole just big enough for the root ball. Always label your plants with the date and variety. Check for pests like cutwormsâplace a collar of cardboard around the stem, sunk 2 cm into the soil.

lessons.title: Minimizing Transplant Shock
lessons.body:
Transplant shock is the stress a seedling suffers when moved. Symptoms include wilting, yellowing leaves, stunted growth, and even death. You can minimize it with careful handling and the right conditions.

First, transplant when the weather is mildâcloudy, humid, or late afternoon. Avoid hot, dry, or windy days. If you must transplant in heat, provide shade for 3 to 5 days using a shade net, palm fronds, or a cardboard tent. Second, keep roots moist at all times. Never let roots dry out. Carry seedlings in a bucket with a little water or wet cloth. Third, disturb roots as little as possible. For tray seedlings, make sure the root ball stays intact. For bare-root, trim damaged roots with clean scissors and dip in a mud slurry.

Fourth, water immediately after transplanting and keep soil consistently moist for the first weekânot soggy. Water daily in the morning for the first 3 days, then every 2 days. Fifth, do not fertilize at transplanting. Wait until new growth appears, then apply a weak liquid fertilizer like compost tea. Sixth, protect from pests and animals. Cutworms can be controlled with a collar. Birds may pull up seedlingsâuse netting or scarecrows.

Seventh, use a starter solution: mix 1 tablespoon of sugar in 1 litre of water and water the seedlings after transplanting. This gives quick energy. Some farmers use a weak solution of seaweed extract. Eighth, if seedlings wilt, do not panicâthey often recover by evening. If they remain wilted for 2 days, shade more and water less to avoid root rot.

Finally, choose the right size seedling. Older seedlings suffer more shock. Always harden off before transplanting. With these steps, your seedlings will establish within 3 to 5 days and start growing strong.

lessons.title: Aftercare for Transplanted Seedlings
lessons.body:
After transplanting, your seedlings need consistent care for the first 2 to 3 weeks. Water is critical. For the first 3 days, water every morning and evening if hot. Then water every 2 days, giving 1 to 2 litres per plant. In sandy soil, water more often; in clay soil, less. Always check the soil: if it's dry 5 cm below the surface, water. If it's soggy, stopâtoo much water causes root rot.

Weed around your seedlings weekly. Weeds compete for nutrients and water. Hand-pull small weeds, or hoe shallowly to avoid damaging roots. Mulch with dry grass, straw, or leaves to suppress weeds and keep moisture. Reapply mulch as it decomposes.

Fertilize only after new leaves appearâusually 7 to 10 days after transplanting. Use a balanced fertilizer like NPK 10-10-10, but dilute it to half strength. For organic growers, apply compost tea or well-rotted manure. Do not put fertilizer directly on the stem; place it 10 cm away. For trees, fertilize after 1 month.

Watch for pests and diseases. Common pests: aphids, whiteflies, cutworms, and caterpillars. Check leaves daily. For aphids, spray with soapy water (1 tablespoon liquid soap in 1 litre water). For cutworms, use collars. For diseases like damping-off, remove affected plants and improve drainage. If you see yellowing leaves, it may be a nutrient deficiency or overwatering.

Provide support for tall plants like tomatoes and peppers. Stake them 2 weeks after transplanting. Use soft ties to avoid cutting stems. For vining crops, provide trellis.

Finally, keep records: date transplanted, number of plants, and any problems. This helps you improve next season. With good aftercare, your seedlings will grow into healthy, productive plants.

lessons.title: Timing Transplanting with Seasons
lessons.body:
Timing is everything. Transplant at the start of the rainy season for most crops. In West Africa, this is April to June; in East Africa, March to May and October to December; in Southern Africa, October to December. For irrigated farming, you can transplant in the dry season, but you must water daily.

Know your first and last frost dates if you are in a highland area. Transplant warm-season crops like tomatoes, peppers, and maize after the last frost. Cool-season crops like cabbage, broccoli, and lettuce can be transplanted 2 to 3 weeks before the last frost. In tropical lowlands, avoid transplanting in the hottest months (e.g., February to March) unless you have shade and irrigation.

Use local signs: when the first rains have soaked the soil 15 cm deep, it's time. When trees like mango or cashew start flowering, it often signals the onset of rains. In drylands, wait for a good downpour that wets the soil to 20 cm. Do not transplant into dry soilâwater the hole first.

For perennial trees, plant at the beginning of the rainy season so they have months to establish before dry season. For short-season crops like lettuce, transplant 4 to 6 weeks before the end of the rains to harvest before heavy pests arrive.

Consider market timing: if you want to sell when prices are high, work backwards. For example, tomatoes take 60 to 80 days from transplant to harvest. If you want to sell in December, transplant in September. Keep a calendar and note weather patterns. Climate change is making seasons less predictable, so be flexible. Always have a backup plan: if rains fail, irrigate. If rains are too heavy, ensure drainage. Talk to experienced farmers in your areaâthey know the best local timing.

quiz.q: How many true leaves should a tomato seedling have before transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Tomato seedlings are typically ready when they have 4 to 6 true leaves, indicating a strong root system.

quiz.q: What is the first sign that a seedling is ready to transplant?
options: B) Roots hold the soil together
quiz.explanation: When roots hold the soil together, the seedling can be lifted without the root ball crumbling.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid transplanting during hot midday sun?
quiz.explanation: Hot sun increases water loss and stress, leading to transplant shock.

quiz.q: How long before transplanting should you start hardening off seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Hardening off should begin 7 to 10 days before transplanting to gradually acclimate seedlings.

quiz.q: What is a key step in hardening off seedlings?
options: D) Keep in full sun all day
quiz.explanation: Reducing water during hardening encourages deeper root growth and toughens plants.

quiz.q: During hardening off, how should you expose seedlings to sun?
quiz.explanation: Gradual exposure prevents scorching and allows plants to adapt to sunlight.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for transplanting tomatoes in the field?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes need 60 cm between plants and 90 cm between rows for good airflow and growth.

quiz.q: When transplanting, how should you handle seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Handling by leaves avoids damaging the delicate stem, which can kill the plant.

quiz.q: For tomatoes, how deep should you plant the seedling?
options: B) Up to first true leaves
quiz.explanation: Burying tomato stems up to the first true leaves promotes additional root growth.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Watering immediately settles the soil around roots and reduces transplant shock.

quiz.q: Which of these helps minimize transplant shock?
options: A) Transplanting on a hot day
quiz.explanation: Keeping roots moist prevents dehydration and reduces stress during transplanting.

quiz.q: What is a starter solution for transplanted seedlings?
quiz.explanation: A weak sugar water solution (1 tablespoon per litre) provides quick energy to stressed seedlings.

quiz.q: How long should you shade transplanted seedlings in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: Shading for 3 to 5 days helps seedlings recover from transplant shock in hot conditions.

quiz.q: What is a sign of transplant shock?
quiz.explanation: Wilting is a common immediate symptom of transplant shock.

quiz.q: When should you first fertilize after transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Fertilizing too early can burn roots; wait until new growth indicates establishment.

quiz.q: How often should you water newly transplanted seedlings in the first 3 days?
options: B) Every morning and evening if hot
quiz.explanation: Frequent watering in the first days helps roots establish and prevents drying out.

quiz.q: What is a good mulch material for transplanted seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Dry grass or leaves are organic mulches that conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

quiz.q: How can you control cutworms after transplanting?
quiz.explanation: A collar of cardboard or plastic around the stem prevents cutworms from cutting seedlings.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to transplant?
quiz.explanation: Late afternoon allows seedlings to settle before the heat of the next day.

quiz.q: For a tree seedling, when is it ready for field transplanting?
options: B) 30-45 cm tall with woody stem
quiz.explanation: Tree seedlings like mango are ready when they reach 30-45 cm and have a woody stem.

quiz.q: In West Africa, when is the main rainy season for transplanting?
quiz.explanation: The main rainy season in West Africa typically starts in April and lasts through June.

quiz.q: What local sign indicates it's time to transplant in drylands?
options: B) First heavy rain soaking soil 20 cm
quiz.explanation: A good downpour that wets the soil deeply signals sufficient moisture for transplanting.

quiz.q: Why is timing transplanting with seasons important?
options: A) To avoid frost and drought
quiz.explanation: Proper timing avoids extreme weather and can align harvest with high market demand.

quiz.q: How can you protect seedlings from frost?
quiz.explanation: Covering seedlings with a blanket or cloth traps heat and prevents frost damage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pot size increase when transplanting to larger containers?
quiz.explanation: A pot 5 cm wider gives roots room to grow without excessive soil that can stay wet.

quiz.q: What is a good potting mix for containers?
options: B) 3 parts soil, 1 part compost, 1 part sand
quiz.explanation: This mix provides good drainage, nutrients, and structure for container-grown seedlings.

quiz.q: How do you harden off bare-root tree seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Root pruning 2 weeks before lifting encourages fibrous roots and reduces transplant shock.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to remove a seedling from a tray?
quiz.explanation: Pushing from the bottom lifts the root ball intact, minimizing damage.

quiz.q: How long does it take for transplanted seedlings to establish?
quiz.explanation: With proper care, most seedlings recover and start new growth within 3 to 5 days.

quiz.q: What should you do if transplanted seedlings remain wilted for 2 days?
options: B) Shade more and water less
quiz.explanation: Prolonged wilting may indicate overwatering; shade and reduce water to prevent root rot.
